title: Activation reuse, distillation compute and representation constraints
subtitle: SAE scaling · OPD versus GRPO · Mechanistic Shaping · Flow Matching
intro: Three readings ask when recycled activations approximate fresh data, where the compute bill for distillation starts, and whether sycophancy remains decodable after its behavior is reduced. Briefs cover test-time compute, data scaling and Muon in practice. The classic is Flow Matching.

articles.paper: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
articles.authors: Nikita Koriagin · Nikita Balagansky · Daniil Gavrilov
articles.title: How much fresh data can reused activations replace?
articles.evidence: Read Sections 4.9–4.12 and Tables 1–2; empirical fit

blocks.text: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) require extracting and storing base-model activations. Applying Muennighoff et al.’s (2023) data-reuse idea to reconstruction, distinguish unique activations U and dictionary width D at fixed exposure T. [1,2]

blocks.label: Empirical conversion: reuse initially approximates fresh data, then each exposure contributes less [1]
EV is explained variance on held-out activations; terms represent insufficient width and effective data [1]

blocks.text: For Llama‑3.1‑8B layer 15 at D=32k and T=640M, the lower endpoint of near-saturation is U=40M for all three SAEs in Table 2, a 16-fold reduction in activation storage.

blocks.title: Boundary
blocks.text: Sparsity differs; compare reuse trends. Storage reduction does not imply end-to-end compute savings, and reconstruction variance does not measure feature interpretability. [1]

articles.paper: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO

articles.title: Distillation can be cheap; where did the teacher come from?
articles.evidence: Read objectives, compute accounting, Sections 5–6 and Appendix J

blocks.text: The student generates its own rollouts. GRPO uses within-group outcome rewards; on-policy distillation (OPD) uses a frozen teacher and renormalizes both distributions over the student’s top 16 tokens at each step. [3]

blocks.tex: \ell_{\rm OPD}=D_{\rm KL}(\widetilde\pi_s\|\widetilde\pi_t),\qquad C_{\rm GRPO}\simeq10N_s T,\qquad C_{\rm OPD}\simeq(10N_s+2N_t)T
blocks.label: T counts each run’s generated tokens; Nₛ and Nₜ count parameters. Teacher forwards add cost; shared prompts are omitted [3]

blocks.text: On math alone, using a GRPO checkpoint of the same Qwen3‑4B‑Base as teacher matched the baseline with about 1/50 of GRPO’s FLOPs in the distillation stage. For multiple domains, the bill starts with training specialists, then merges them into a fresh Qwen3‑4B‑Base. [3]

headers: Total FLOPs saved at matched score

blocks.title: Boundary
blocks.text: Matched scores are against the authors’ instance-mixed joint GRPO. External-teacher failures depend on the recipes tested, and FLOPs are not wall-clock time. [3]

articles.paper: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
articles.authors: Satchel Grant · Michael Byun (blog); Thomas Fel et al. (paper)
articles.title: After behavior changes, can a probe still decode the concept?
articles.dateNote: Blog 2026-11-05; paper first posted 2026-11-04 14:29 EST · v1
articles.evidence: Read blog, paper framework, DPO comparisons and Figure 14

blocks.text: Output rewards alone do not specify what a decision should rely on. The authors add a representation penalty to the task objective and distinguish concept expression from reliance. [4,5]

blocks.label: Minimization form of the framework: task loss plus a representation penalty [5]
Illustration with fixed unit concept direction v: expression in activation z on the left, local sensitivity of readout s on the right

blocks.text: The OLMo‑3‑7B sycophancy experiment adds a directional attribution penalty to DPO. The original fixed difference-of-means probe’s AUROC falls from 0.981 to 0.931; freely refitted linear probes still recover the signal at evaluated training steps. [4,5]

blocks.title: Boundary
blocks.text: Failure of a fixed probe does not show erasure, and successful refitting in this experiment does not ensure monitoring under distribution shift. [5]

classic.authors: Yaron Lipman · Ricky T. Q. Chen · Heli Ben-Hamu · Maximilian Nickel · Matt Le
classic.title: Why does regressing conditional velocities learn the marginal flow?
classic.dateNote: ICLR 2023; first arXiv posting and version read: v1, 2022-10-06
classic.evidence: Read Sections 2–4 and Appendix A; squared-error decomposition is an explanatory derivation

recognition.label: ICLR 2023 · Historical work on continuous generative modeling (official record checked 2026-11-06)

classic.question: At fixed training sample count and endpoint error, how would you separately compare conditional-velocity regression noise and sampling ODE solver cost?

blocks.text: Neural ODEs (2018) formulate generation as continuous dynamics; score SDEs (2021) use noising paths to construct a training target. Flow Matching regresses velocities directly and samples a single path point during training. Draw data Y∼q, independent base noise X₀∼N(0,I), and uniform time t. [20,21]

blocks.tex: p_t(x)=\int p_t(x\mid y)\,q(dy),\qquad u_t(x)=\mathbb E[u_t(X_t\mid Y)\mid X_t=x]
blocks.label: Theorem 1: average conditional velocities under the posterior wherever the density is positive [20]
Continuity equation: under the paper’s smoothness conditions, integrating conditional flux gives marginal flux [20]
Regression interpretation of Theorem 2: the conditional residual has mean zero given (t,Xₜ), so the cross term vanishes [20]
Conditional Gaussian OT path: each noise sample follows a straight line; terminal noise has scale σₘᵢₙ [20]
Integrate the learned ODE at sampling time [20]

blocks.title: Boundary
blocks.text: Conditional OT does not imply marginal OT after mixing. With σₘᵢₙ>0 the ideal endpoint is data smoothed by small Gaussian noise; finite-step integration adds separate error. [20]
